questions.question: Which reaction occurs when an alkoxide ion attacks a primary alkyl halide via SN2 mechanism?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Williamson synthesis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Williamson synthesis** is a reaction in which an **alkoxide ion reacts with a primary alkyl halide** via an **SN2 mechanism** to form an ether. This method is widely used in organic chemistry for ether synthesis.
 
• In this reaction, the **alkoxide ion** (R-O⁻) acts as a nucleophile and attacks the electrophilic carbon atom of the primary alkyl halide (R'-X), resulting in the formation of an ether (R-O-R').
 
• This reaction follows a **bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) mechanism**, which is characterized by a single-step process where the nucleophile attacks the substrate and displaces the leaving group simultaneously.
 
• The reaction is most efficient when the alkyl halide is **primary** because primary alkyl halides are less sterically hindered, making it easier for the nucleophile to attack.
 
• **Secondary and tertiary alkyl halides** are less suitable for Williamson synthesis due to steric hindrance and the possibility of side reactions such as elimination.
 
• The choice of solvent plays a crucial role in the reaction. Polar aprotic solvents like **dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)** or **acetone** are often used to enhance the nucleophilicity of the alkoxide ion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mechanism of SN2 Reaction:**

 
 
• In an SN2 reaction, the nucleophile attacks the carbon atom attached to the leaving group from the opposite side, leading to the displacement of the leaving group.
 
• The reaction results in an **inversion of configuration** at the carbon center, often referred to as a "backside attack."
 
• SN2 reactions are highly sensitive to steric hindrance, which is why they are most effective with **primary alkyl halides**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Alkoxide Ions:**
 
 
• Alkoxide ions (R-O⁻) are strong nucleophiles due to their negatively charged oxygen atom, which has a high electron density.
 
• They are typically generated by reacting alcohols with a strong base like **sodium hydride (NaH)** or **potassium hydroxide (KOH)**.
 
• Examples include sodium ethoxide (C2H5ONa) and potassium tert-butoxide (t-BuOK).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Williamson Synthesis:**
 
 
• This reaction is widely used in industrial and laboratory settings to synthesize **simple and mixed ethers**.
 
• For example, diethyl ether (CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3) can be synthesized by reacting sodium ethoxide with ethyl bromide.
 
• The reaction is also used to synthesize **complex aromatic ethers**, such as anisole (C6H5-O-CH3).
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• **Arndt-Eistert synthesis:** This is a method used to elongate carboxylic acids by one carbon atom, involving diazomethane. It has no relevance to ether formation.
 
• **Friedlaender synthesis:** This is a reaction for synthesizing quinoline derivatives, not ethers.
 
• **Coumarin synthesis:** This is a method for synthesizing coumarins, a class of organic compounds with a benzopyrone structure, unrelated to ether formation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Primary Alkyl Halides:** These are compounds where a halogen atom is attached to a carbon atom bonded to only one other carbon atom. They are ideal for SN2 reactions due to minimal steric hindrance.
 
• **Leaving Groups:** The leaving group (e.g., halide ions like Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) should be stable and capable of dissociating easily to facilitate the reaction.
 
• **Side Reactions:** With secondary or tertiary alkyl halides, elimination reactions (E2 mechanism) can compete with substitution, leading to by-products.
 
• **Environmental Considerations:** Some alkyl halides and solvents used in Williamson synthesis can be toxic or harmful to the environment, necessitating proper handling and disposal.

questions.question: Jharkhand has announced its first tiger safari in the Barwadih Western Forest Range; it is a part of which tiger reserve?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Palamau Tiger Reserve**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jharkhand** has announced its first-ever tiger safari in the **Barwadih Western Forest Range**, which is a part of the **Palamau Tiger Reserve**.
 
• The **Palamau Tiger Reserve** is located in the **Latehar district** of Jharkhand and is one of the first nine tiger reserves established in India under the **Project Tiger initiative in 1973.**
 
• The reserve is a major contributor to wildlife conservation in India and is known for its rich biodiversity, including species like **tigers, elephants, leopards, and sloth bears**.
 
• Palamau Tiger Reserve is spread across an area of approximately **1,129.93 sq. km**, with a core area of 414.93 sq. km and a buffer area of 715 sq. km.
 
• The establishment of the tiger safari in this reserve aims to boost **eco-tourism** and raise awareness about **tiger conservation**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Palamau Tiger Reserve:**

 
 
• The Palamau Tiger Reserve is part of the **Betla National Park**, which is a popular tourist destination known for its scenic beauty and wildlife.
 
• It is located in the **Chota Nagpur Plateau** and is characterized by **dry deciduous forests**, sal trees, and bamboo groves.
 
• It was the first tiger reserve in India to introduce **tiger census using pugmark tracking**.
 
• The reserve faces conservation challenges, including the threat of poaching, human-wildlife conflict, and habitat degradation.
 
 
 
• **Project Tiger:**
 
 
• Launched in **1973**, Project Tiger is a flagship conservation program of the Indian government aimed at protecting **tigers and their habitats**.
 
• The project is administered by the **National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)**.
 
• India is home to approximately **70% of the world’s tiger population**, and the project has been instrumental in increasing the tiger population in the country.
 
 
 
• **Other Tiger Reserves in India:**
 
 
• **Bandipur Tiger Reserve:** Located in Karnataka, it is part of the **Niligiri Biosphere Reserve** and is known for its diverse flora and fauna.
 
• **Sanjay Gandhi Tiger Reserve:** Situated in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, it is known for its dense forests and tiger population.
 
• **Pench Tiger Reserve:** Spread across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, it inspired Rudyard Kipling’s **"The Jungle Book."**
 
 
 
• **Importance of Tiger Reserves:**
 
 
• Tiger reserves play a vital role in conserving **India’s biodiversity** and maintaining ecological balance.
 
• They contribute to eco-tourism, providing economic benefits to the local communities.
 
• Tigers are a **keystone species**, and their conservation ensures the protection of other flora and fauna in their habitat.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eco-Tourism and its Benefits:**

 
 
• The establishment of tiger safaris and reserves promotes **eco-tourism**, which helps in generating revenue and employment for the local population.
 
• It also raises awareness about the importance of **wildlife conservation** and encourages sustainable practices.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Tiger Conservation:**
 
 
• The major threats include **poaching, habitat loss, and human encroachment**.
 
• Climate change and forest degradation also pose significant challenges to tiger populations.
 
• Efforts like relocation of villages from core areas and stricter anti-poaching measures are being implemented to address these challenges.

questions.question: Hills of Kaimur, the easternmost part of the Vindhya Range, which begins near Jabalpur districts of Madhya Pradesh, ends near which district of Bihar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rohtas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Kaimur Hills**, forming the easternmost extension of the **Vindhya Range**, stretch from **near Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh** and conclude in the **Rohtas district of Bihar**.
 
• The Vindhya Range is one of the oldest mountain ranges in India, known for its rich geological and geographical significance.
 
• The Kaimur Hills are a prominent plateau region, often considered a natural extension of the Vindhyan ranges.
 
• In the Rohtas district, the Kaimur Hills are home to several historical and natural sites, including the **Rohtasgarh Fort**, cascading waterfalls, and lush vegetation.
 
• The range is significant for its rich reserves of **limestone and other minerals**, as well as for being a hotspot for biodiversity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kaimur Hills:**

 
 
• The Kaimur Hills form a part of the Vindhyan escarpment, which is geologically ancient and primarily composed of sandstone and quartzite.
 
• These hills are spread across the Indian states of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar, with their easternmost tip in the Rohtas district.
 
• The Kaimur range is known for its natural beauty, including waterfalls like **Karkat Waterfall** and wildlife sanctuaries like the **Kaimur Wildlife Sanctuary**.
 
 
 
• **Vindhya Range:**
 
 
• The Vindhya Range runs parallel to the Narmada River in central India and holds immense geographical and cultural importance.
 
• It serves as a natural divide between northern and southern India, influencing climatic and vegetation patterns.
 
• Rich in minerals like limestone, sandstone, and bauxite, this range contributes significantly to India's economy.
 
 
 
• **Rohtas District:**
 
 
• Rohtas is a district in the state of Bihar, historically known for the **Rohtasgarh Fort**, a site of archaeological and historical importance.
 
• The district is part of the Kaimur plateau and is known for its fertile soil, making it an important agricultural region.
 
• Rohtas is also home to significant rivers like the **Sone River**, a tributary of the Ganges.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• The Kaimur region, including Rohtas, has been a center of cultural and historical activity, with evidence of human habitation dating back to ancient times.
 
• Important historical landmarks include ancient rock paintings, inscriptions, and temples.
 
 
 
• **Geological Importance:**
 
 
• The Kaimur Hills are part of the Vindhyan Supergroup, which is significant for studying the Earth's early history, including paleoclimate and tectonic activity.
 
• They also contain fossilized remains of ancient flora and fauna, contributing to paleontological research.

questions.question: What is the disintegration of rocks into smaller fragments without any change in their chemical composition called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mechanical Weathering**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mechanical weathering** refers to the physical disintegration of rocks into smaller fragments without any alteration in their chemical composition.
 
• It occurs due to external physical forces such as **temperature changes, abrasion, pressure, frost action, and biological activities**.
 
• Some common processes of mechanical weathering include **frost wedging, exfoliation, and thermal expansion.**
 
• Unlike chemical weathering, mechanical weathering does not involve chemical reactions or the formation of new minerals.
 
• This type of weathering is prevalent in areas with extreme temperature variations, such as **deserts, polar regions, and high-altitude zones.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Exfoliation:**

 
 
• Exfoliation is a process of mechanical weathering where successive layers of rock peel off or crack due to temperature changes or pressure release.
 
• This phenomenon is common in areas with large temperature fluctuations, such as deserts.
 
 
 
• **Block Disintegration:**
 
 
• Block disintegration occurs when large blocks of rock break apart due to repeated freezing and thawing cycles or pressure changes.
 
• It is prominent in cold climates where water enters cracks in rocks, freezes, and expands, causing the rock to split.
 
 
 
• **Frost Action:**
 
 
• Frost action is a type of mechanical weathering caused by the freezing and thawing of water in rock cracks.
 
• When water freezes, it expands by approximately **9%**, exerting pressure on the rock and causing it to fracture.
 
• This process is common in polar regions and high-altitude areas.
 
 
 
• **Thermal Expansion:**
 
 
• Thermal expansion occurs when rocks experience temperature changes, causing the minerals within the rock to expand and contract at different rates.
 
• This leads to stress and eventual disintegration of the rock surface.
 
 
 
• **Biological Weathering:**
 
 
• Although not purely mechanical, biological weathering can contribute to physical disintegration. Roots of plants penetrate rock cracks, exerting pressure and causing fragmentation.
 
• Animals also contribute by burrowing into rocks and soil, aiding in their disintegration.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference Between Mechanical and Chemical Weathering:**

 
 
• Mechanical weathering involves physical processes, while chemical weathering involves chemical reactions.
 
• Mechanical weathering does not change the chemical composition of rocks; chemical weathering forms new minerals.
 
• Examples of chemical weathering include **oxidation, hydrolysis, and carbonation.**
 
 
 
• **Applications of Mechanical Weathering:**
 
 
• It plays a crucial role in soil formation by breaking down rocks into smaller particles.
 
• Mechanical weathering contributes to shaping landscapes, including the formation of valleys, cliffs, and plains.
 
• It aids in the natural recycling of minerals and nutrients in ecosystems.
 
 
 
• **Significance in Geology:**
 
 
• Understanding mechanical weathering is essential for studying geological processes like erosion and sedimentation.
 
• It helps in predicting the stability and durability of rock formations in construction and mining industries.

questions.question: The United Kingdom has signed an agreement to hand over Chagos Island to which of the following countries?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mauritius**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Chagos Archipelago**, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, was a British overseas territory known as the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT).
 
• The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) passed a resolution in **2019** urging the United Kingdom to return the Chagos Archipelago to **Mauritius**. This resolution was supported by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
 
• Mauritius has long claimed sovereignty over the Chagos Islands, which were separated from Mauritius by the UK in **1965** before Mauritian independence in **1968**.
 
• The UK signed an agreement in **2023** to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius as part of a broader reconciliation effort in response to international legal and diplomatic pressure.
 
• The transfer agreement is a significant step towards addressing colonial-era injustices and respects Mauritius' sovereignty under international law.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chagos Archipelago:**

 
 
• The Chagos Archipelago consists of over **60 islands** located in the Indian Ocean, about **500 km south of the Maldives**.
 
• The archipelago is strategically important due to its location between Africa and Asia, and houses a major US military base on **Diego Garcia**.
 
• Chagos' indigenous population, known as the **Chagossians**, were forcibly removed by the UK in the **1960s and 1970s** to make way for the military base.
 
 
 
• **Mauritius' Claim:**
 
 
• Mauritius claims the Chagos Archipelago as part of its territory based on historical, legal, and geographical factors.
 
• The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (**UNCLOS**) and other international rulings support Mauritius' claim.
 
 
 
• **International Court of Justice (ICJ) Ruling:**
 
 
• In **2019**, the ICJ ruled that the UK's continued administration of the Chagos Islands was unlawful and that the UK should return the islands to Mauritius.
 
• The ICJ's advisory opinion highlighted the principle of self-determination and the illegality of the UK's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius before independence.
 
 
 
• **UNGA Resolution:**
 
 
• Following the ICJ's ruling, the UNGA passed a resolution with overwhelming support, urging the UK to withdraw from the Chagos Archipelago and hand over control to Mauritius.
 
• This resolution emphasized the importance of respecting international law and decolonization processes.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Importance of Chagos:**
 
 
• The Chagos Archipelago is strategically located in the Indian Ocean and plays a key role in global maritime security.
 
• The US military base on Diego Garcia is a critical hub for operations in the Middle East, Africa, and Asia.

questions.question: Which of the following methods is used to rename a file or folder in MS Windows?

options.text: Double-click the file to open it

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right-click the file and select 'Rename'.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Renaming files or folders in MS Windows** is a crucial operation that helps in organizing and managing files effectively.
 
• The easiest and most common method to rename a file or folder is to **right-click** on the respective file or folder and select the 'Rename' option from the context menu.
 
• After selecting 'Rename,' the file or folder name becomes editable. Users can type the desired new name and press 'Enter' to save the changes.
 
• Renaming files helps in maintaining clarity, especially in cases where multiple files of similar content are stored together.
 
• This method works across all modern versions of **Microsoft Windows**, including Windows 10 and Windows 11, and is user-friendly.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other methods to rename files/folders in MS Windows:**

 
 
• **Using F2 Key:** Select the file or folder and press the **F2 key** on the keyboard to rename it. This is a quick shortcut for renaming.
 
• **Using File Explorer:** Navigate to the file or folder in File Explorer, click once on the name, or use the 'Home' tab and select the 'Rename' option in the ribbon.
 
• **Command Prompt:** Advanced users can use the **rename** command (or **ren** command) in Command Prompt to rename files or folders programmatically.
 
 
 
• **Common Mistakes:**
 
 
• **Double-clicking:** Double-clicking on a file opens it rather than renaming it. This is a common misunderstanding among beginners.
 
• **Keyboard shortcuts:** 'Ctrl + R' is not a valid shortcut for renaming files. Instead, the F2 key is widely used for this purpose.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Renaming:**
 
 
• Helps in maintaining file organization and improves workflow efficiency.
 
• Essential for file identification, especially in projects involving multiple contributors or large datasets.
 
 
 
• **Supported File Systems:** Renaming functionality is supported in all major file systems used by Windows, such as **NTFS, FAT32, and exFAT**.
 
• **Best Practices:** Avoid using special characters (e.g., , :, ", /, \, |, ?, *) in file names, as they are not allowed in Windows file systems and can lead to errors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Context Menu:** The right-click context menu in Windows provides various options, such as 'Rename,' 'Delete,' 'Copy,' and 'Properties,' which make file management convenient.
 
• **Undo Renaming:** If a file is renamed by mistake, users can press **Ctrl + Z** to undo the change immediately.
 
• **Batch Renaming:** Windows also allows batch renaming of multiple files by selecting all desired files, right-clicking, and selecting 'Rename.' The files will receive a common base name with sequential numbers appended.

questions.question: Which of the following factors most influences the uneven distribution of population in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Soil fertility and water availability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Soil fertility** and **water availability** are the most significant factors influencing the uneven distribution of population in India. Fertile lands support intensive agriculture, which, in turn, sustains a large population. For example, the **Indo-Gangetic Plains**, with fertile alluvial soil and abundant water from rivers like the Ganges and Yamuna, have a high population density.
 
• Regions with **scarce water resources** or infertile soil, such as parts of the **Thar Desert** in Rajasthan, tend to have lower population densities. The lack of agricultural potential and water scarcity makes these areas less habitable.
 
• Access to water resources is critical not only for agriculture but also for drinking, sanitation, and industrial activities, which are essential for sustaining large populations. For instance, regions near perennial rivers like the Brahmaputra and Godavari have dense populations.
 
• Fertile regions can produce more food, which attracts people for better livelihood opportunities. This is evident in states like **Punjab** and **Haryana**, which are known for their agricultural productivity and have high population densities.
 
• Conversely, areas with poor soil quality, such as rocky plateaus or arid regions, face challenges in sustaining large populations. For example, the Deccan Plateau has a relatively lower population density due to less fertile soil compared to the Indo-Gangetic belt.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Language Diversity:**

 
 
• Language diversity does not significantly influence population distribution. While it impacts cultural identity and social cohesion, it does not determine where people choose to live.
 
• India, with its **22 official languages** and numerous dialects, showcases a rich linguistic diversity across states, but this does not directly affect population density.
 
 
 
• **Trade Union Policies:**
 
 
• Trade union policies are more relevant to industrial and labor relations and have limited impact on population distribution.
 
• Urban areas with significant industrial activity, such as Mumbai or Chennai, might see some influence of trade unions, but this is not a major determinant in overall population distribution.
 
 
 
• **National Income:**
 
 
• While high national income can lead to better infrastructure and living standards, which may attract people to certain regions, it is not the primary factor in population distribution.
 
• For example, despite India's GDP growth, rural areas with fertile land and water resources remain densely populated compared to many urban centers.
 
 
 
• **Soil Fertility and Water Availability:**
 
 
• These natural factors are the primary determinants of population distribution. Regions with favorable agricultural conditions and dependable water resources can support larger populations.
 
• For example, **Kerala** and **West Bengal**, with fertile soils and abundant water, have high population densities.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Population Distribution in India:**
 
 
• The **Indo-Gangetic Plains** have a population density of over 1,000 people per square kilometer due to fertile soil and a reliable water supply.
 
• The **Thar Desert** in Rajasthan has a sparse population due to arid conditions and lack of water resources.
 
• The **Northeastern states**, despite rich natural resources, have lower population densities due to rugged terrain and limited agricultural potential.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of Rivers:** Rivers like the Ganga, Yamuna, and Brahmaputra not only provide water for agriculture but also support industries and urban settlements, contributing to high population densities in adjacent regions.
 
• **Climate:** Favorable climates, such as the tropical monsoon climate of India, support agriculture and enhance the habitability of regions with fertile soil and water resources.
 
• **Urbanization:** Cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru attract populations due to industrial and economic opportunities, but their population densities are still influenced by proximity to water and agricultural productivity in surrounding areas.
 
• **Technological Advancements:** In some arid or less fertile regions, advancements in irrigation and agriculture, such as in parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan, have enabled higher population densities.

questions.question: Which of the following combinations of shortcut keys and functions is correctly matched?

options.text: Ctrl + Tab – Copies the selected text
Ctrl + C – Copies content to the clipboard
Ctrl + F – Switches between open tabs
Ctrl + V – Finds a specific word in the document

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ctrl + C – Copies content to the clipboard**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ctrl + C – Copies content to the clipboard:** This is the standard shortcut used to copy text, images, or other content to the clipboard. Once copied, the content can be pasted elsewhere using the **Ctrl + V** command. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Ctrl + Tab – Copies the selected text:** This shortcut is used to switch between open tabs in browsers or applications, not for copying text. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Ctrl + F – Switches between open tabs:** This shortcut is primarily used to open the "Find" dialog to search for specific words or phrases within a document or webpage. It does not switch between tabs. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Ctrl + V – Finds a specific word in the document:** This shortcut is used to paste the content from the clipboard. It does not perform the "Find" function. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Clipboard Functionality:**

 
 
• The clipboard temporarily stores the copied content (text, images, files) until it is pasted elsewhere.
 
• It is an essential feature of operating systems and helps in transferring data efficiently between applications.
 
 
 
• **Common Keyboard Shortcuts:**
 
 
• **Ctrl + X:** Cuts the selected content and moves it to the clipboard.
 
• **Ctrl + Z:** Undoes the last action performed in most applications.
 
• **Ctrl + Y:** Redoes the last undone action.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Ctrl + C:**
 
 
• Used in text editors (e.g., Notepad, MS Word) to copy text.
 
• Widely used in design software (e.g., Photoshop, Illustrator) to duplicate objects or layers.
 
• Functional across operating systems like **Windows, macOS** (Command + C), and Linux.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Keyboard Shortcuts:**
 
 
• Enhances productivity by reducing dependency on mouse clicks.
 
• Improves accessibility for users with physical disabilities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference between Copy (Ctrl + C) and Cut (Ctrl + X):**

 
 
• **Copy:** Duplicates the selected content and keeps it in the original location.
 
• **Cut:** Removes the selected content from its original location and places it in the clipboard.
 
 
 
• **MacOS Shortcuts:**
 
 
• Instead of Ctrl, macOS uses the Command key for shortcuts. For example:
 
• **Command + C:** Copy.
 
• **Command + V:** Paste.
 
• **Command + X:** Cut.

questions.question: Which Indian judgment laid down the concept of ‘Basic Structure’ of the Constitution?

options.text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The concept of the **‘Basic Structure’** of the Constitution was first propounded in the landmark case of **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**. This judgment is considered one of the most significant in Indian constitutional history.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that while the Parliament has vast powers under **Article 368** of the Indian Constitution to amend the Constitution, it cannot alter or destroy its **basic structure**.
 
• The judgment introduced the doctrine that certain fundamental features of the Constitution, such as **democracy, rule of law, separation of powers, and judicial review**, are inviolable and cannot be amended.
 
• The case arose when the Kerala government passed laws to regulate land ownership and impose land reforms, which were challenged by the petitioner, Kesavananda Bharati, on the grounds that they violated his fundamental rights.
 
• This judgment limited the Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and protected the spirit of the Indian Constitution from being eroded by arbitrary amendments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Landmark Cases Related to Constitutional Amendments:**

 
 
• **Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967):** The Supreme Court ruled that **Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights**. This decision was later overturned in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
• **Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980):** This case reaffirmed the doctrine of the basic structure and held that a balance between **Fundamental Rights** and **Directive Principles** is part of the Constitution's basic structure.
 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978):** This case expanded the interpretation of **Article 21**, emphasizing that the right to life and personal liberty cannot be curtailed except by a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable.
 
 
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:**
 
 
• Examples of elements within the **basic structure** include **sovereignty, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and judicial independence**.
 
• The doctrine ensures that constitutional amendments cannot alter the essence of the Constitution, preserving its core values and framework.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Kesavananda Bharati Case:**
 
 
• It introduced a mechanism for judicial review of constitutional amendments to ensure they align with the Constitution's basic structure.
 
• It marked a turning point in Indian constitutional law, emphasizing the supremacy of the Constitution over parliamentary authority.
 
• This case is often regarded as the **‘savior of the Constitution’**, ensuring the protection of fundamental rights and democratic principles.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Article 368:**
 
 
• Article 368 provides the **power to amend the Constitution**, but the Kesavananda Bharati judgment clarified that this power is not absolute and is subject to judicial review.
 
• The article plays a critical role in maintaining the Constitution's flexibility while ensuring its core principles are preserved.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Parliamentary Authority vs. Judicial Review:**

 
 
• The Kesavananda Bharati judgment struck a balance between the **amending power of Parliament** and the **judicial review power of the judiciary**.
 
• The ruling emphasized that neither Parliament nor the judiciary is supreme, but the **Constitution is the ultimate authority**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Judicial Independence:**
 
 
• The judgment reinforced the independence of the judiciary as a guardian of the Constitution, ensuring checks and balances in governance.
 
• This independence is critical for upholding the rule of law and protecting the rights of citizens.

questions.question: Which law states that a compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Law of Definite Proportions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Law of Definite Proportions**, also known as the **Law of Constant Composition**, was proposed by **Joseph Proust** in **1799**.
 
• This law states that a chemical compound always contains its component elements in a **fixed ratio by mass**, regardless of the source or how the compound is prepared.
 
• The law applies to pure chemical compounds, ensuring that the proportion of elements remains consistent. For example, in water (H₂O), the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen by mass is always **1:8**.
 
• It is an essential principle in **stoichiometry**, the calculation of reactants and products in chemical reactions.
 
• This law is foundational to modern chemistry, as it establishes the concept that compounds are made of elements combined in specific proportions, laying the groundwork for the development of chemical formulas and molecular theory.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Law of Conservation of Mass:**

 
 
• Proposed by **Antoine Lavoisier** in **1789**, it states that **mass is neither created nor destroyed** in a chemical reaction.
 
• This law is fundamental to balancing chemical equations and understanding that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
 
• Example: In the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water, the total mass of hydrogen and oxygen is equal to the mass of water produced.
 
 
 
• **Law of Multiple Proportions:**
 
 
• Proposed by **John Dalton** in **1803**, it states that when two elements form more than one compound, the ratios of the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in **small whole numbers**.
 
• Example: Carbon and oxygen form two compounds: carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). The ratio of oxygen masses in CO and CO₂ is 1:2.
 
 
 
• **Avogadro’s Law:**
 
 
• Proposed by **Amedeo Avogadro** in **1811**, it states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of molecules.
 
• This law is critical to understanding the behavior of gases and is the basis for the concept of the **mole** in chemistry.
 
• Example: One mole of any gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP) occupies a volume of **22.4 liters**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of the Law of Definite Proportions:**
 
 
• The law is used in determining the **empirical formula** of compounds.
 
• It helps in **quality control** during the synthesis of chemical compounds.
 
• It is a fundamental concept in **analytical chemistry**, ensuring the purity of chemical substances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Law of Definite Proportions** applies only to **pure substances** and not to mixtures.
 
• This law is sometimes considered a precursor to the modern atomic theory, as it implies that matter is composed of discrete units (atoms).
 
• Joseph Proust’s experiments with compounds like copper carbonate and tin oxides demonstrated the consistency of element ratios, providing empirical evidence for this law.
 
• While the law is universally true for chemical compounds, exceptions can occur in non-stoichiometric compounds, where the ratio of elements can vary slightly.

questions.question: Which tribal revolt in 1831-32 was led by Buddho Bhagat and targeted exploitative landlords and British officials?

__
 
• The **Kol Revolt** occurred during **1831-32** and was one of the earliest tribal uprisings against British rule in India.
 
• The revolt was primarily led by **Buddho Bhagat**, a tribal leader who mobilized the Kols against the **exploitative landlords** and **British officials**.
 
• The uprising was triggered by the **introduction of new revenue policies** and the increasing oppression of tribal lands by landlords and moneylenders under British rule.
 
• The Kols were known for their fierce resistance and organized attacks, which targeted **British officers**, government officials, and landlords in the region.
 
• The rebellion was eventually suppressed by the British forces, but it highlighted the growing discontent among tribal communities due to exploitative practices and the erosion of their traditional rights.

__
 
• **Kol Revolt:**

 
 
• The Kols were an indigenous tribal community residing in areas like **Chotanagpur** in present-day Jharkhand.
 
• The rebellion was a reaction to the exploitation brought by **British revenue policies**, which led to the forced acquisition of their lands and the imposition of high rents.
 
• Other tribal leaders and communities also joined the revolt, making it a significant uprising in tribal history.
 
• The revolt marked the beginning of tribal resistance movements in India against British colonial policies.
 
 
 
• **Bhil Revolt:**
 
 
• The **Bhil Revolt** occurred in **1822** in the western regions of India, primarily in **Maharashtra** and **Rajasthan**.
 
• It was led by Bhil leaders like **Rama Naik** and revolved around grievances related to **land alienation** and exploitation under British rule.
 
• Unlike the Kol Revolt, the Bhils were more spread out and focused on guerrilla warfare against British forces.
 
 
 
• **Munda Revolt:**
 
 
• The **Munda Revolt** was led by **Birsa Munda** in **1899-1900** and occurred in the region of **Chotanagpur Plateau**.
 
• This uprising was motivated by socio-religious reforms and the protection of tribal lands from encroachment by landlords and British officials.
 
• Birsa Munda emerged as a spiritual leader and called for the establishment of Munda Raj.
 
 
 
• **Santhal Revolt:**
 
 
• The **Santhal Revolt**, also known as the **Santhal Hul**, occurred in **1855-56** and was led by **Sido and Kanhu Murmu**.
 
• The revolt was against the exploitation by **zamindars**, moneylenders, and British policies in the Santhal Parganas region.
 
• It was one of the largest tribal uprisings in colonial India and led to significant changes in British policies towards tribal communities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Tribal Revolts:**

 
 
• Tribal revolts like the **Kol Revolt** brought attention to the exploitation and marginalization faced by indigenous communities under British rule.
 
• They demonstrated the fierce resistance of tribal communities and their determination to protect their lands, culture, and rights.
 
• These uprisings forced the British administration to reconsider their policies and implement changes to address tribal grievances.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Tribal Revolts:**
 
 
• Most tribal revolts were rooted in issues like **land alienation**, **high rents**, and exploitation by landlords and moneylenders.
 
• Leaders like **Buddho Bhagat**, **Birsa Munda**, and **Sido Murmu** played pivotal roles in mobilizing their communities.
 
• These movements were often suppressed by British forces but left a lasting legacy in India's struggle against colonial rule.

questions.question: Who among the following is eligible to be appointed as the Chairperson of the Lokpal, as per the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013?

options.text: A retired Cabinet Secretary of India
A sitting judge of a High Court
A former Judge of the Supreme Court

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A former Judge of the Supreme Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013** establishes the Lokpal as an anti-corruption ombudsman to investigate complaints of corruption against public officials and government organizations.
 
• As per Section 3 of the Act, the **Chairperson of the Lokpal** must be either a current or former **Chief Justice of India**, a **Judge of the Supreme Court**, or an **eminent person** with expertise in anti-corruption, public administration, or law.
 
• The option "**A former Judge of the Supreme Court**" aligns with the eligibility criteria outlined in the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, making it the correct answer.
 
• Individuals such as **retired Cabinet Secretaries**, **sitting High Court Judges**, or **Members of Parliament** are not eligible to serve as Chairperson under the Act.
 
• The Lokpal Chairperson is appointed by a selection committee that includes the Prime Minister, Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Leader of the Opposition, the Chief Justice of India, or a Supreme Court judge nominated by the CJI.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013:**

 
 
• The Act was enacted to set up an independent institution called Lokpal at the central level and Lokayukta at the state level to investigate cases of corruption against public functionaries.
 
• The Lokpal consists of a **Chairperson** and a maximum of **eight members**. Out of these, 50% must be judicial members, and at least 50% of the total members must belong to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, minorities, or women.
 
 
 
• **Eligibility Criteria for Chairperson:**
 
 
• The Chairperson must have served as the Chief Justice of India, a Supreme Court Judge, or an eminent person with specialized knowledge and experience in anti-corruption, public administration, or related fields.
 
• The Chairperson or members are appointed for a term of **5 years** or until they reach the age of 70, whichever is earlier.
 
 
 
• **Selection Committee:**
 
 
• The committee responsible for appointing the Chairperson and members consists of:
 
 
• The Prime Minister (Chairperson).
 
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by the CJI.
 
• An eminent jurist recommended by the President.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Functions of Lokpal:**
 
 
• Lokpal is empowered to investigate cases of corruption against the Prime Minister, Ministers, Members of Parliament, Group A, B, C, and D government officials, among others.
 
• The Lokpal can direct any central agency like the CBI to investigate cases under its jurisdiction.
 
• It ensures accountability and transparency in governance by addressing complaints of corruption and taking suitable actions.
 
 
 
• **Exclusions:**
 
 
• Members of Parliament concerning anything said or votes cast in Parliament are excluded from the jurisdiction of the Lokpal.
 
• The Lokpal cannot inquire into allegations against the Prime Minister about international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• The demand for a Lokpal in India began in the 1960s, inspired by the Ombudsman system in Scandinavian countries.
 
• The **First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)**, in its report in 1966, recommended setting up a Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas at the state level.
 
 
 
• **First Lokpal Appointment:**
 
 
• **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose** was appointed as the first Lokpal of India in **March 2019**.
 
 
 
• **Key Features:**
 
 
• The Lokpal has jurisdiction over all Members of Parliament, Ministers, and public servants, including Group A, B, C, and D officials.
 
• The institution is intended to strengthen the anti-corruption framework in the country.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Central Goods and Services Tax Act enacted?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2017**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act** was enacted in the year **2017** by the Government of India.
 
• The Act forms a crucial part of the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** framework, which was introduced to create a unified tax regime across India, replacing various indirect taxes.
 
• The **CGST Act**, along with the **State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) Act**, **Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) Act**, and the **Union Territory Goods and Services Tax (UTGST) Act**, came into effect on **1st July 2017**.
 
• The GST regime was implemented under the provisions of the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**, which empowered both the Centre and the States to levy and collect GST.
 
• The CGST Act governs the taxation of intra-state supply of goods and services and ensures that the Centre collects the respective share of tax revenue.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **What is Goods and Services Tax (GST)?**

 
 
• **GST** is a comprehensive indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services across India.
 
• The tax is designed to eliminate the cascading effect of taxes, i.e., "tax on tax," and to streamline the taxation process.
 
• It is a destination-based tax, meaning the tax revenue is collected by the state in which the goods or services are consumed.
 
 
 
• **Structure of GST:**
 
 
• The GST framework in India is divided into three main categories:
 
• **Central GST (CGST):** Levied by the Central Government on intra-state supplies.
 
• **State GST (SGST):** Levied by the respective State Governments on intra-state supplies.
 
• **Integrated GST (IGST):** Levied by the Central Government on inter-state supplies.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of CGST Act:**
 
 
• Defines provisions for the levy and collection of **CGST** on intra-state supplies.
 
• Outlines the rules for input tax credit, registration, and the filing of returns.
 
• Provides for penalties, audits, and appeals for non-compliance with tax regulations.
 
 
 
• **101st Constitutional Amendment Act:**
 
 
• This amendment paved the way for the implementation of GST by introducing **Article 246A**, which grants concurrent powers to both the Centre and States to legislate on GST.
 
• It also established the **GST Council**, a constitutional body responsible for recommending GST rates, exemptions, and other related policies.
 
 
 
• **Implementation Timeline:**
 
 
• The GST was formally launched on **1st July 2017** by the then President of India, **Pranab Mukherjee**, and the Prime Minister, **Narendra Modi**.
 
• It replaced multiple indirect taxes such as **VAT, service tax, excise duty, and more**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **GST Council:**

 
 
• It is a statutory body chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes State Finance Ministers as members.
 
• The Council makes recommendations on issues such as tax rates, exemptions, and GST laws.
 
 
 
• **Impact of GST:**
 
 
• It has significantly simplified the taxation process by subsuming multiple indirect taxes under a single framework.
 
• GST is expected to enhance the ease of doing business and increase tax compliance in India.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in GST Implementation:**
 
 
• Initial challenges included adapting to the new system, addressing technical glitches, and ensuring compliance from businesses.
 
• Over time, the system has evolved with improvements such as the introduction of e-invoicing and simplification of GST returns.

questions.question: In which year was the first cases of the disease now known as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) identified?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1981**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The first cases of the disease now known as **Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)** were identified in the **United States in 1981**.
 
• In **June 1981**, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a report describing cases of a rare lung infection, **Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP)**, in five young, previously healthy gay men in Los Angeles.
 
• During the same period, cases of a rare cancer, **Kaposi’s sarcoma**, were reported in young gay men in New York and California. These conditions signaled the emergence of a new, unknown disease.
 
• The term **AIDS** was coined in **1982**, and the disease was recognized as a severe weakening of the immune system caused by an infection.
 
• In **1983**, researchers identified the virus responsible for AIDS, now known as the **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV):**

 
 
• HIV is the virus that causes AIDS. It attacks the body’s **immune system**, specifically the **CD4 cells** (T cells), which help the immune system fight infections.
 
• Without treatment, HIV reduces the number of CD4 cells in the body, making the person more vulnerable to infections and certain cancers.
 
• HIV is primarily spread through **unprotected sexual contact**, sharing of needles, transfusion of contaminated blood, and from mother to child during childbirth or breastfeeding.
 
 
 
• **Global Impact:**
 
 
• AIDS has caused a global pandemic, with millions of people affected worldwide since its discovery in 1981.
 
• According to **UNAIDS**, as of **2023**, approximately **38 million people** are living with HIV worldwide.
 
• Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region most severely affected, with an estimated **two-thirds** of all people living with HIV located in this region.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Treatment:**
 
 
• Key prevention strategies include **safe sex practices**, use of **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** for HIV-positive individuals, and education on reducing transmission risks.
 
• ART does not cure HIV but can **control the virus**, enabling individuals to live longer, healthier lives and reducing the risk of transmission.
 
• The development of **pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)** and **post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)** has further advanced HIV prevention.
 
 
 
• **Milestones in HIV/AIDS Research:**
 
 
• The first HIV test, known as the **ELISA test**, was developed in **1985**.
 
• The first antiretroviral drug, **AZT (zidovudine)**, was approved for use in **1987**.
 
• In **1996**, the advent of combination antiretroviral therapy, also known as **Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART)**, revolutionized treatment and significantly improved life expectancy for HIV-positive individuals.
 
 
 
• **Global Initiatives:**
 
 
• **UNAIDS** was established in **1996** to coordinate the global response to the AIDS pandemic.
 
• The **90-90-90 targets** were introduced to ensure that by **2020**, 90% of people living with HIV would know their status, 90% of those diagnosed would receive treatment, and 90% of those treated would achieve viral suppression.
 
• In **2021**, new targets were set to ensure **95-95-95** by 2030 to end the AIDS epidemic as a public health threat.

questions.question: The Pallava kings adopted which title to reflect that their rule was guided by the principles of the Dharmashastras?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dharma-Maharaja**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Pallava kings adopted the title **Dharma-Maharaja** to signify that their governance was guided by the principles of **Dharmashastras**, which are ancient Hindu scriptures outlining moral and ethical conduct.
 
• The term **Dharma** refers to righteousness, moral law, and duty, emphasizing the ethical responsibilities of rulers to uphold justice, fairness, and societal welfare.
 
• By using the title **Dharma-Maharaja**, Pallava rulers highlighted their commitment to ruling in accordance with **Hindu philosophical traditions** and maintaining the sanctity of governance.
 
• The Pallava dynasty was known for its contributions to art, architecture, and religious values, evident in structures such as the **rock-cut temples of Mahabalipuram**.
 
• Other titles like **Maharajadhiraja** and **Chakravarti** were common among Indian monarchs, but **Dharma-Maharaja** specifically underscored the Pallavas’ adherence to spiritual and ethical principles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pallava Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Pallavas ruled South India from the **3rd to 9th century CE**.
 
• They were prominent in regions corresponding to modern-day **Tamil Nadu** and parts of **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• The Pallavas are renowned for fostering **Hindu culture, literature, and temple architecture**.
 
• Examples of their architectural marvels include the **Shore Temple** and **Pancha Rathas** at Mahabalipuram.
 
 
 
• **Dharmashastras:**
 
 
• The Dharmashastras are ancient Hindu texts composed in Sanskrit that provide guidelines on **law, ethics, and social duties**.
 
• They cover topics like governance, justice, societal roles, and the moral obligations of individuals.
 
• Important Dharmashastras include texts like the **Manusmriti** and **Yajnavalkya Smriti**.
 
• The Pallavas likely adopted teachings from these texts to ensure a righteous and ethical rule.
 
 
 
• **Titles of Indian Kings:**
 
 
• **Maharajadhiraja:** This title translates to "king of kings" and was used to signify supremacy over other rulers.
 
• **Chakravarti:** Refers to an emperor or universal ruler, emphasizing territorial dominance and political authority.
 
• **Dharma-Maharaja:** This unique title indicates adherence to moral and ethical governance, as seen in the Pallava dynasty.
 
• **Rajadhiraja:** Indicates a high-ranking monarch, often subordinate to Maharajadhiraja.
 
 
 
• **Mahabalipuram:**
 
 
• Mahabalipuram, also known as Mamallapuram, is famous for its **UNESCO World Heritage-listed monuments**.
 
• The site includes **rock-cut temples, caves, and sculptures** that reflect Pallava art and architecture.
 
• These monuments were primarily constructed during the reign of **Narasimhavarman I**, a notable Pallava ruler.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hindu Philosophy:** The principles of governance during the Pallava dynasty were deeply influenced by Hindu philosophical traditions like the **concept of Dharma**, which emphasizes righteous conduct.
 
• **Legacy:** The Pallavas left a profound impact on Indian culture through their contributions to **religion, art, and architecture**.
 
• **Education and Literature:** Pallava rulers patronized scholars and encouraged the development of **literature**, particularly in Tamil and Sanskrit.
 
• **Temple Architecture:** The Pallavas pioneered the **Dravidian style** of temple construction, a hallmark of South Indian architecture.

questions.question: What is the tenure duration of Justice BR Gavai as the Chief Justice of India?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Justice B.R. Gavai** was appointed as the **Chief Justice of India (CJI)** on **May 19, 2023**, succeeding Justice D.Y. Chandrachud.
 
• The tenure of Justice B.R. Gavai as the Chief Justice of India is notably short, lasting for a period of **6 months**. He is set to retire on **November 23, 2023**, upon reaching the retirement age of 65 years as per the Constitution of India.
 
• As per Article **124(2) of the Indian Constitution**, a Supreme Court judge, including the Chief Justice of India, serves until they attain the age of **65 years**.
 
• The short tenure of Justice Gavai underscores the rotational nature of appointments to the position of Chief Justice of India, which ensures that senior judges of the Supreme Court get the opportunity to serve as CJI.
 
• Justice Gavai is the **second Dalit Chief Justice** of India after Justice K.G. Balakrishnan, making his appointment historically significant in terms of representation in the judiciary.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Appointment of the Chief Justice of India:**

 
 
• The Chief Justice of India is appointed by the **President of India** under Article **124(2)** of the Constitution.
 
• The appointment is based on the **seniority principle** among the judges of the Supreme Court.
 
• Before appointing the Chief Justice, the outgoing CJI traditionally recommends their successor to the President.
 
 
 
• **Tenure and Retirement:**
 
 
• The retirement age for Supreme Court judges, including the Chief Justice, is **65 years**, as per the Constitution.
 
• The tenure of a Chief Justice may vary depending on their age at the time of appointment, often leading to some CJIs having relatively short terms.
 
• Justice B.R. Gavai’s tenure is an example of such a short term, as he is set to retire in **November 2023**, six months after his appointment.
 
 
 
• **Justice B.R. Gavai’s Career Highlights:**
 
 
• Justice Gavai began his judicial career in the **Bombay High Court**, where he served as a judge for over a decade.
 
• He was elevated to the Supreme Court of India on **May 24, 2019**.
 
• Justice Gavai has delivered several landmark judgments during his career and is known for his expertise in constitutional and civil law.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• Justice Gavai is the **second Dalit Chief Justice** of India, following Justice K.G. Balakrishnan, highlighting the importance of inclusivity in the judicial system.
 
• His appointment signifies the commitment to ensuring representation of all communities in the higher judiciary, contributing to the principles of social justice enshrined in the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The judiciary in India is guided by the principles of **independence, impartiality, and inclusivity**, and the appointment of Chief Justices reflects these values.
 
• The Chief Justice of India plays a pivotal role as the head of the judiciary and the administrative head of the Supreme Court, ensuring the smooth functioning of the judicial system.
 
• Short tenures of CJIs, such as that of Justice Gavai, demonstrate the rotational system that allows multiple senior judges to serve as the head of the judiciary, upholding the principle of equality and fairness.

questions.question: The 91st Amendment of the Indian Constitution was enacted in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2003**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **91st Amendment** to the **Indian Constitution** was enacted in the year **2003**. This amendment holds significant importance in ensuring political stability and reducing defections in Indian politics.
 
• It introduced changes to the **Tenth Schedule** of the Constitution, which deals with the **anti-defection law**. This amendment strengthened the provisions to discourage political defections.
 
• The amendment made it mandatory that the size of the **Council of Ministers**, including the Prime Minister or Chief Minister, should not exceed **15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha or the respective State Legislative Assembly**.
 
• The **anti-defection law** was also tightened by disallowing disqualification exemptions in case of splits involving less than one-third of the members of a political party.
 
• The **91st Amendment Act** was a response to growing concerns about political instability caused by defections and bloated cabinets, which often led to inefficiency and wastage of public resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Anti-Defection Law**:

 
 
• Introduced through the **52nd Amendment Act of 1985**, the anti-defection law was included in the **Tenth Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
• It aimed to curb political defections by disqualifying members who defected from their parties after elections.
 
• The **91st Amendment** further strengthened the provisions of the anti-defection law by removing the loophole that allowed splits involving one-third of a party's members.
 
 
 
• **Size of the Council of Ministers**:
 
 
• Before the **91st Amendment**, there was no constitutional limit on the size of the Council of Ministers, which led to unwieldy and bloated cabinets.
 
• The amendment introduced a cap, limiting the size of the Council of Ministers to **15% of the total strength** of the Lok Sabha or the State Legislative Assembly.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the 91st Amendment**:
 
 
• It promoted **political stability** by discouraging defections and ensuring that elected representatives stayed loyal to their parties.
 
• The limitation on the size of cabinets ensured **efficiency** and reduced the burden on public finances.
 
• The amendment reinforced the principles of **democracy** and accountability by holding legislators accountable for their actions.
 
 
 
• **Other Constitutional Amendments Related to Political Reforms**:
 
 
• The **52nd Amendment** (1985) introduced the anti-defection law in the Tenth Schedule.
 
• The **73rd and 74th Amendments** (1992) provided constitutional status to **Panchayati Raj Institutions** and Urban Local Bodies, respectively.
 
• The **97th Amendment** (2011) recognized the **right to form cooperatives** as a fundamental right under Article 19.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Background of the 91st Amendment:**

 
 
• The amendment was introduced in response to the growing menace of political defections and the practice of forming oversized cabinets to accommodate defectors.
 
• The political scenario in the late 20th century witnessed frequent instability due to defections, leading to the need for stricter laws.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Amendment:**
 
 
• The amendment has been instrumental in ensuring political stability in both the central and state governments.
 
• It has reduced the practice of offering ministerial positions to legislators as an incentive for defection.

questions.question: Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas in states, other than the Northeast?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fifth Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Fifth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution pertains to the **administration and control of Scheduled Areas** and **Scheduled Tribes** in states other than the Northeastern states.
 
• It provides for the establishment of a **Tribes Advisory Council** (TAC) in each state having Scheduled Areas. These councils advise on matters related to the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes.
 
• The **President of India** is empowered to declare certain areas as Scheduled Areas and can also modify or rescind such declarations. The administration of these areas is subject to special provisions.
 
• The **Governor** of the state, under the Fifth Schedule, has the authority to make regulations for the peace and good governance of these areas, including restricting land transfers and regulating the allotment of land to members of Scheduled Tribes.
 
• The Fifth Schedule ensures the protection of tribal interests, particularly in terms of their **land rights** and **cultural heritage**, by incorporating specific provisions for their governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sixth Schedule:**

 
 
• The Sixth Schedule pertains to the administration of **tribal areas** in the **Northeastern states**, including Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
• It provides for the formation of **Autonomous District Councils** (ADCs) that have legislative, judicial, and executive powers to govern the tribal areas autonomously.
 
• The ADCs have the power to make laws on various subjects such as land management, forest conservation, water resources, and village administration.
 
 
 
• **Ninth Schedule:**
 
 
• The Ninth Schedule was introduced by the **First Amendment Act, 1951** to protect laws related to **land reforms** and the abolition of the zamindari system from being challenged in courts.
 
• Laws placed under this schedule are immune from judicial review, even if they violate fundamental rights, as per Article 31B of the Constitution.
 
• However, the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** clarified that laws under the Ninth Schedule can be reviewed if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Seventh Schedule:**
 
 
• The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution delineates the division of powers between the **Union and State governments** through three lists: the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
 
• Subjects in the **Union List** are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the central government, while those in the **State List** fall under state jurisdiction. Subjects in the **Concurrent List** are shared by both the Union and State governments.
 
• Examples of subjects under these lists include defense (Union List), police (State List), and education (Concurrent List).
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• Scheduled Areas are defined as areas that are **predominantly inhabited by Scheduled Tribes** and require special protection and governance due to their socioeconomic conditions.
 
• The Fifth Schedule applies to states such as **Rajasthan, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, and Jharkhand**, where tribal populations are significant.
 
• The provisions under this schedule aim to maintain a balance between the preservation of tribal culture and traditions and the integration of these communities into mainstream society.

questions.question: What does globalisation mainly mean in economic terms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Connecting to the world economy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** in economic terms refers to the integration of a country's economy with the global economy, characterized by the free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, and labor across international borders.
 
• It involves the reduction of trade barriers and tariffs, allowing countries to engage in **international trade** and investment freely.
 
• Globalisation promotes **economic interdependence**, leading to increased cooperation among nations for mutual benefits, such as economic growth, technological advancements, and cultural exchange.
 
• The concept includes the establishment of global supply chains, where production processes are spread across different countries to optimize costs and efficiency.
 
• Major institutions like the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**, and **World Bank** play a critical role in fostering and regulating globalisation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Globalisation:**

 
 
• **Free Trade:** Reduction of tariffs and import-export restrictions to facilitate trade between nations.
 
• **Technological Integration:** Adoption and exchange of advanced technologies globally, boosting innovation and industrial growth.
 
• **Economic Integration:** Merging of financial markets, international investments, and the establishment of multinational corporations.
 
• **Global Supply Chains:** Goods and services are sourced and produced in multiple countries, leveraging comparative advantages.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of Globalisation:**
 
 
• Enhances **economic growth** by providing access to larger markets and international investments.
 
• Encourages cultural exchange and the sharing of ideas, values, and traditions.
 
• Boosts technological advancement through global collaboration and competition.
 
• Creates job opportunities by attracting foreign direct investment (FDI).
 
 
 
• **Challenges of Globalisation:**
 
 
• **Income Inequality:** Disparities in wealth distribution between developed and developing nations.
 
• **Loss of Cultural Identity:** Overemphasis on global culture may overshadow local traditions and practices.
 
• **Environmental Concerns:** Increased industrialization and transportation contribute to pollution and climate change.
 
• **Dependency Risks:** Over-reliance on global supply chains may lead to vulnerabilities during crises (e.g., COVID-19 pandemic).
 
 
 
• **Globalisation in India:**
 
 
• India embraced globalisation in **1991** with the introduction of the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms under the leadership of **Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• These reforms significantly opened up India's economy to foreign trade and investment, fostering economic growth.
 
• India became a member of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** in **1995**, further integrating with the global economy.
 
• Key sectors impacted include **IT, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, and services**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Globalisation Milestones:**

 
 
• The establishment of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** in **1995** to oversee global trade rules.
 
• The creation of regional trade agreements like the **European Union (EU)**, **NAFTA** (now USMCA), and **ASEAN**.
 
• The rise of multinational corporations like **Apple, Amazon, and Toyota**, reflecting economic interdependence.
 
 
 
• **Globalisation and Technology:**
 
 
• Technological advancements in communication (e.g., **the internet**) have accelerated globalisation.
 
• **E-commerce** platforms like **Amazon** and **Alibaba** enable global trade at an unprecedented scale.

questions.question: The five village committees (variyams) such as neernilai variyam and needhi variyam were a unique administrative feature of which of the following dynasties?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pandyas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Pandyas** were one of the prominent dynasties of ancient South India, known for their unique administrative systems, including the establishment of village-level governance through committees.
 
• The five **village committees (variyams)**, such as **Neernilai Variyam** (water management committee) and **Needhi Variyam** (justice committee), were integral to their governance. These committees played significant roles in managing local affairs and ensuring efficient administration.
 
• The **Neernilai Variyam** was responsible for regulating water resources, reflecting the agrarian nature of the society and the importance of irrigation in South India during the Pandya rule.
 
• The **Needhi Variyam** served as a judicial body to resolve disputes and ensure justice at the village level, showcasing a structured approach to legal administration.
 
• The Pandya dynasty, flourishing during the **6th to 14th centuries CE**, was headquartered in regions like **Madurai** and was instrumental in fostering art, culture, and architecture alongside administrative innovations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Features of Pandya Administration:**

 
 
• The Pandya kings had a well-organized **centralized administration**, with a king as the supreme authority.
 
• Local administration was divided into **nadus** (regional divisions) and further subdivided into **villages**, with village assemblies playing a crucial role in governance.
 
• The village committees (**variyams**) were highly specialized in their functions, such as irrigation, justice, taxation, and temple management.
 
• Their administrative structure was deeply influenced by democratic principles, with active participation of local people in decision-making processes.
 
 
 
• **Other Dynasties for Comparison:**
 
 
• **Guptas:** Known as the "Golden Age" of India (4th to 6th century CE), the Gupta Empire was famous for advancements in **science, mathematics, and literature**, but they did not have the unique village committees like the Pandyas.
 
• **Satavahanas:** The Satavahanas (2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE) had a centralized administrative system with provincial governors, but their governance did not emphasize village-level committees as seen in the Pandya dynasty.
 
• **Mauryas:** The Mauryan Empire (321–185 BCE) had a highly centralized administrative structure with royal officials overseeing provinces, but village-level committees were not a notable feature of their governance.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Village Committees:**
 
 
• These committees ensured **localized governance**, efficient resource utilization, and a participatory approach to administration.
 
• They also reflect the agrarian focus and self-sustaining nature of ancient Indian villages.
 
• Such systems highlight the advanced administrative thinking of ancient Indian rulers like the Pandyas, who emphasized inclusivity and specialization in governance.
 
 
 
• **Pandya Legacy:**
 
 
• The Pandyas were patrons of **Sangam literature**, which provides valuable insights into their administrative, social, and cultural practices.
 
• Their contributions to temple architecture, such as the **Meenakshi Temple** in Madurai, underline their emphasis on art and religion.
 
• Their efficient governance system, including the village committees, laid the foundation for future administrative models in South India.

questions.question: Where and when is the final in‑flight testing of the Kaveri Derivative Engine (KDE) scheduled, as part of its certification process?

__

• The final **in-flight testing** of the engine is scheduled to take place in **Russia**, a country with advanced aerospace testing facilities, by **late 2025**.
 
• The selection of **Russia** for testing highlights the collaborative ties between India and Russia in defense and aerospace technologies.
 
• This step is crucial as it will ensure that the engine meets all necessary operational and safety standards before being certified for use in aircraft.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kaveri Engine Development:**

 
 
• The Kaveri engine project was initiated in the **1980s** by the **Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE)**, a DRDO lab, to develop an indigenous engine for India's fighter jets.
 
• Despite technological challenges, the Kaveri program laid the foundation for advancements in indigenous gas turbine technology.
 
 
 
• **Collaboration with Russia:**
 
 
• India and Russia have a longstanding relationship in defense and aerospace, with Russia providing technical expertise and infrastructure for testing and evaluation.
 
• Russia’s advanced testing facilities are critical for the rigorous evaluation of the KDE under real-world conditions.
 
 
 
• **Applications of the Kaveri Derivative Engine:**
 
 
• The KDE is expected to be used in **Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)** and other aerial platforms, enhancing India’s self-reliance in defense technology.

• **Importance of In-Flight Testing:**
 
 
• In-flight testing is essential to verify the performance, reliability, and safety of the engine under various operational conditions.
